items.ms: Level of response, 6 marks: up to 4 for indicative content plus up to 2 for structure and linkages. Key points: methane has only London forces; London forces are weaker than hydrogen bonds; NH3, H2O and HF have hydrogen bonds; London forces are similar because the electron numbers are the same; F is the most electronegative so the H-F bond is the most polar; water has more hydrogen bonds per molecule (2:1) than NH3 or HF, hence the highest boiling temperature.

items.name: Boiling temperatures of F2, HCl and methanol
items.how: Level-of-response (*) question: explain the large variation in the boiling temperatures of fluorine, hydrogen chloride and methanol despite their similar Mr values; detailed descriptions of the forces are not required (the methanol boiling temperature is missing from the input text).
items.ms: Level of response, 6 marks (up to 4 for indicative points plus 2 for structure and reasoning). Points: F2 is non-polar so has only London forces; HCl is polar (Cl more electronegative than H) with permanent dipole interactions as well as London forces; methanol has H on a small electronegative atom (O) so forms hydrogen bonds; hydrogen bonds are the strongest forces and need most energy to break; London forces are the weakest so F2 has the lowest boiling temperature.

items.ms: Level of response, 6 marks (up to 4 for indicative points plus 2 for structure and reasoning). items.ms: (a)(i) fewer gas moles on the right so high pressure favours methanol (or more collisions raise the rate); (ii) exothermic so low temperature favours yield, a compromise temperature gives a fast enough rate; (iii) catalyst allows lower temperature or is selective/reusable. items.name: Compare heterogeneous and homogeneous transition metal catalysis

items.ms: Level of response (up to 4 marks for indicative points plus up to 2 for structure and lines of reasoning). Indicative points: both lower the activation energy by an alternative route; heterogeneous catalyst is in a different phase from the reactants and is easy to separate, homogeneous is in the same phase and harder to separate; a named heterogeneous example and reaction (Fe in the Haber process, Ni in alkene hydrogenation, Pt in a catalytic converter); a named homogeneous example (Fe2+/Fe3+ with iodide and peroxodisulfate ions); heterogeneous mechanism by adsorption onto the surface, bond weakening, reaction and desorption (or V2O5 reduced to V(IV) and re-oxidised in the Contact process); homogeneous mechanism by the transition metal ion being oxidised or reduced and then returning to its original oxidation state. Non-transition-metal examples or incorrect reactions are not credited.
